{"id":"gen-1794670090-vcfFa6YKV8Mi98YDBdjI","object":"chat.completion","created":1794670090,"model":"deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017","provider":"Ionstream","system_fingerprint":null,"service_tier":null,"choices":[{"index":0,"logprobs":null,"finish_reason":"stop","native_finish_reason":"stop","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{
  "rating": 0.55,
  "explanation": "The combined regime is split. At the national layer the traveller meets the sharpest exposure: passport sex-marker rules, an 'X' marker no longer processed, a February 2025 cable directing officers to refuse cases with document discrepancies and to weigh lifetime ineligibility for material misrepresentation, and documented abuse in immigration custody. Those follow every visitor at the border. Inside the division, however, the operative picture is genuinely protective: public-accommodation law covering gender identity with an enforcement body, no facility ban, open marker-change rules, functioning hate-crime enhancement, and a most-protective risk tier. The division's protections do not reach the national border desk or national custody, so the score sits in the Elevated band — materially better than a criminalising jurisdiction, materially below a jurisdiction whose working protections also cover entry and custody.",
  "factor_matrix": {
    "entry_documents": {
      "exposure": "National executive order bars self-selected markers and foreign-ministry processing of X markers; February 2025 cable directs officers to refuse cases with document discrepancies and consider lifetime ineligibility for material misrepresentation.",
      "protection": "Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; misrepresentation finding is never automatic and requires four elements; litigation ongoing and some orders enjoined.",
      "interaction": "Division's open state documents do not reach national passport or visa issuance; the traveller clears national, not division, document rules at the border.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "investigation_detention_custody": {
      "exposure": "Immigration custody documents forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of transgender men; national corrections policies impose conversion-style practices.",
      "protection": "A legal-aid organisation maintains a FAQ on passport and identity-document rules; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity.",
      "interaction": "A document discrepancy at entry can flow into national detention, where the division's anti-discrimination law has no purchase.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "federal_state_facilities": {
      "exposure": "National order bars transgender people from federally funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; 9 states ban facility use in all government buildings, 4 criminalise certain bathroom use in public buildings.",
      "protection": "This division has no facility ban; its public-accommodations law covers facilities, and its risk tier is the most-protective tier.",
      "interaction": "A visitor staying within the division avoids the facility bans, but transiting or crossing into a neighbouring jurisdiction enters a materially different environment.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "care_services": {
      "exposure": "National orders target gender-affirming care for minors; travel insurance and emergency care questions for outed travellers are unresolved.",
      "protection": "April 2023 state executive order directs agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming care within the division, including for people travelling in; hospital records must protect gender-identity data.",
      "interaction": "The division's shield reaches in-division providers but the dossier does not describe its effect on out-of-division subpoenas or on national facilities.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "threat_framing_law_enforcement": {
      "exposure": "National counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups as a priority; national rhetoric frames gender ideology as extremist, and a rewards memorandum uses that phrase.",
      "protection": "Division bars discrimination, bars the panic defence, and the chief legal office sued school boards whose policies out trans students.",
      "interaction": "National threat framing does not control the division's police, but it colours the national border and investigative layer the traveller passes through.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "minors_guardians": {
      "exposure": "National executive order directs law enforcement to investigate schools facilitating a minor's social transition and to prosecute teachers; national care bans for minors apply in 27 states.",
      "protection": "This division has no such ban; its guidance promotes name/pronoun policies, and its chief legal office litigated against parental-notification policies.",
      "interaction": "A parent travelling with a trans minor child would face national border and custody exposure but a protective division environment for schools and services.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "street_violence_police_response": {
      "exposure": "National hate-crime reporting for gender identity is uneven across states; the criminalisation of bathroom use in some states creates arrest risk for the visibly trans.",
      "protection": "Division has bias-crime enhancements, sensitivity training, a police-licensing system of gender-identity protections, and ranks among the safest per-capita measured rates; the panic defence is barred.",
      "interaction": "Violence data show legal hostility does not predict where trans women are killed; the division's own combination of low violence and working protections is the operative picture inside its borders.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "remedies_unknowns": {
      "exposure": "Lifetime ineligibility and refusal-of-entry decisions are discretionary and appeal-dependent; the passport suits and executive-order challenges are unresolved.",
      "protection": "A division civil-rights enforcement body investigates and can grant relief; legal aid maintains guidance on the national rules.",
      "interaction": "The traveller's remedy for an adverse border decision lies in the national system, not the division's, so the strong local remedies do not reach the exposure",
      "status": "documented"
    }
  },
  "anchor_checks": [
    {
      "anchor_id": "0.35-A",
      "comparison": "Both involve denial at the border with an administrative regime and no detention. This case is worse: the national cable also contemplates a lifetime ineligibility finding and the dossier documents abusive immigration custody, both above the anchor's mere exclusion and confiscation, so it rates above."
    },
    {
      "anchor_id": "0.55-B",
      "comparison": "Comparable: an adverse administrative flag is worked through a written guideline with a supervisor's intervention, giving a temporary permit and no detention. Here the adverse flag is national and discretionary rather than appealable on the spot, but the division offers real service and accommodation recourse, so the rating is similar."
    },
    {
      "anchor_id": "0.75-C",
      "comparison": "In that anchor the privacy directive worked in the encounter and the director apologised, and the only risk was a downstream legacy database. Here the operative authority at the border is the restrictive national rule, not the division's protective law, so this case sits materially lower."
    }
  ],
  "synthesis": "The traveller experiences two regimes stacked. The national layer owns the border, document screening, visa framing and immigration custody, and there it holds the whole exposure: a visitor flagged on mismatched or unavailable markers may be questioned, refused or found permanently ineligible, and any detention that follows falls under a custody record documented as abusive. The division layer owns daily life, and there it is close to the best available: public accommodation, lodging, care, facilities, hate-crime remedies and low measured violence. Neither layer is role of law-free, but a division's local enforcement cannot follow the traveller to the national desk, and the local exposure does not match the national burden, so that the score sits above the hostile facially unrestricted options and below the low-risk options."
}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"Parent national framework is restrictive in traveler-facing ways: passport markers, entry screening, trans athletes ban, facility bans in some states, custody harm. Division evidence is protective: anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, facilities open, hate-crime, ID documents open, protective tier.

Combined operative regime: national border/entry rules govern every visitor (passport sex-marker mismatch, visa fraud risk), national facility bans don't apply at the division level but state bans are in some states. This division is highly protective.

Score must sit below comparable independent jurisdiction? No, this is a subnational dossier within a national framework. Under V3, the combined operative regime is rated. The division's protective laws do not cancel national entry screening and national enforcement. So the score must be materially below what the division would score alone.

National entry: passport markers restricted, X not processed, customs screening, discrepancy instructions to refuse and request evidence, possible permanent ineligibility for fraud. That's a real traveler-facing exposure — risk of denial of entry, secondary screening, invasive questions. Plus detention/custody harm for immigration custody, and national facility restrictions in some states.

However division: anti-discrimination protections in public accommodations, ID documents open, no bathroom ban, no state criminalization, protective tier, low violence. Local police and facilities treat trans people fine.

So what's the number? National exposures: denial of entry (severity 3), invasive screening, possible fraud finding (severe). Not a criminalization; no imprisonment for being trans per se, but detention in immigration custody with documented abuse. Divisional protections work for lodging, services, care.

I'd put it around 0.55–0.65. Compare anchors: 0.55-A/D — protections with ombudsman work, but continued logged flag. 0.65 anchors — protections function, but public friction. 0.75 — documented charter recognized, clear.

Here the division has real working protections (relief granted, enforcement body), and the state has no facility bans, but the national border regime creates an unavoidable universal-exposure measure at entry: document marker scrutiny, X-marker not recognized, discretionary refusal and potential lifetime fraud finding. That is a tier-1-ish universal exposure for international visitors. Also custody conditions in immigration detention documented (severe). That drags down.

But note the visitor arriving on a home passport with mismatched marker — most trans travelers from abroad would be flagged; but the rating isn't probability of outing, it's consequences. Consequences: refusal of entry, invasive secondary, possible lifetime ineligibility; not arrest or imprisonment for being trans. Also, the facilities bans apply in 9+ states but not this one.

I'd give ~0.55. Hmm, the division has strong protections including accommodation access, hate crime, healthcare access. Combined with national border risk: refusal of entry is severity 3, and immigration detention is documented with abuse (severity 4-5) though that's for those in custody.

Let me consider anchors: 0.55-A is "administrative alternative to detention, ombudsman intervenes, no prolonged holds, but logged in system." Similar-ish. 0.65-A is "charter requires acceptance of self-declared markers; inspector delays; protection worked." Here the national rule is the opposite: marker must match birth sex; X not processed. So the border exposure is heavier than 0.65-A.

0.45-A: ombudsman exists but non-binding, denial of boarding, no detention, manifest flagged. That's roughly comparable in mildness but here the consequences (refusal of entry, permanent fraud finding) are worse.

I'd settle 0.52–0.58. Let's say 0.55. Actually, weighing: entry exposure is documented, universal (every visa/passport check under the new rule plus the February cable instructing officers to refuse where discrepancy and consider lifetime ineligibility). That's a strong traveler-facing exposure, plus documented immigration custody abuse. But within the country, the state-level protections are excellent — accommodations, care, hate crime, no facility bans, low violence.

The division's protections do not cancel national border screening. So the score sits elevated. I'll go 0.52.

Hmm. Let me think about the band: 0.40-0.60 Elevated Risk. That fits: a place where a traveler whose documents mismatch may be denied entry or heavily questioned, but where, once in, facilities, services, and care are protected and violence is low. I'll say 0.55.

Actually maybe slightly higher, since a visitor with a passport correctly matching their presentation and documentation would likely be fine, and the interior is highly protective. But the rubric says don't credit passing. The marker rule means trans visitors whose documents don't match birth sex... actually the rule is about US-issued passports; a foreign passport's marker is whatever home country issued. But the cable says where discrepancy in documents or records or evidence casting doubt on sex, refuse and request evidence. So foreign trans visitors with X markers may face refusal. Judges §"Entry screening carries its own exposure." So material.

I'll set 0.55.

Anchors: 0.35-A (denial of entry, documents confiscated, no detention), 0.55-A (ombudsman release, logged), 0.75-C (privacy directive, staff apology, working protection). And maybe 0.65-B.
